item.mechanism: Creep deformation is dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
item.supporting_observation: Stress exponent of 5 to 6 and activation energy of 268 kJ mol−1, which is comparable to lattice diffusion of constituent elements (288–317 kJ mol−1).
item.scope_limits: Does not fully explain the abnormally high stress exponents (8.9–14) observed in the high-stress region (HSR).
item.alternatives_considered: Dislocation glide or climb mechanisms typically responsible for stress exponents of 3 to 5.
quotes: The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1

The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion is suggested as a possible rate-dominating mechanism at low stresses.

records.text: Mechanism with scope. Mechanism: Creep deformation is dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Mn20). Conditions: Low-stress region (LSR), 500–600 °C, 140–200 MPa. Evidence: measured. Observation: Stress exponent of 5 to 6 and activation energy of 268 kJ mol−1, which is comparable to lattice diffusion of constituent elements (288–317 kJ mol−1).. Scope limits: Does not fully explain the abnormally high stress exponents (8.9–14) observed in the high-stress region (HSR).. Alternatives: Dislocation glide or climb mechanisms typically responsible for stress exponents of 3 to 5.. Quote: "The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1"

item.mechanism: Abnormally high stress exponents in the high-stress region are caused by the coordinative contributions of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic precipitation.
item.supporting_observation: Observation of dynamic recrystallization, refined grain sizes, and nano-sized precipitates (M23C6 and Cr-rich σ phase) along grain boundaries.
item.scope_limits: The authors note that dynamic recrystallization alone is insufficient to explain the stress exponent increase; precipitation hardening must also be involved.
item.alternatives_considered: Power-law breakdown assumption, which was deemed inappropriate as no deviation from linear relationships was observed.
quotes: Nevertheless, the abnormally high stress exponents in HSR were ascribed to the coordinative contributions of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic precipitation.
The anomalously high stress exponent and activation energy in HSR were attributed to the combinative effects of dynamic recrystallization and precipitation.
However, this value is still higher than those for traditional solid solution alloys, which implies that the sole recrystallization is insufficient and additional mechanisms should be involved.

item.mechanism: Dynamic precipitates act as barriers for dislocation motion, increasing the activation energy for creep deformation.
item.supporting_observation: Identification of M23C6 carbides and Cr-rich σ phase precipitates along grain boundaries with sizes of 50–200 nm.
item.scope_limits: Difficult to precisely estimate the boundary obstacle stress due to ambiguous interaction between dynamic precipitation and recrystallization.
item.alternatives_considered: None explicitly stated as alternatives for the barrier effect, but the text notes the difficulty in quantifying the stress reduction.
quotes: In particular, the precipitates act as barriers for dislocation motion via producing boundary obstacle stress, resulting in high activation energy for creep deformation.
The precipitates are predominantly formed along the grain boundaries and would exert a boundary obstacle stress σ b o , which prevent the annihilation of moving dislocations at the boundaries.

item.mechanism: Dynamic recrystallization leads to grain refinement, which increases the stress exponent by altering the grain size dependence of creep.
item.supporting_observation: Grain size reduction from ~25 μm (initial) to ~22 μm (500 °C/400 MPa) and ~31 μm (600 °C/320 MPa), with volume fraction of small equiaxed grains increasing.
item.scope_limits: Calculated stress exponent increase from recrystallization alone (~7.5) is still higher than traditional solid solution alloys, indicating it is not the sole cause.
item.alternatives_considered: Grain boundary sliding, which is mentioned as a consequence of recrystallization but not the primary driver of the high stress exponent.
quotes: Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels.
It is documented that dynamic recrystallization during the creep process could cause an increase in the stress exponent.

item.mechanism: Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations indicate active dislocation climb and high dislocation density.
item.supporting_observation: TEM observations showing dislocation jogging, tangling, and looped configurations in both stress regions.
item.scope_limits: Observed in both LSR and HSR, but the density and configuration differ significantly between regions.
item.alternatives_considered: None explicitly stated, but the text contrasts the limited dislocation activity in LSR with the high density in HSR.
quotes: Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively.
The observed jog configurations are indicative of a dislocation climb process.
In contrast, the dislocations in HSR exhibit a higher density of configurations. Numerous short straight segments are tangled and tend to form cell substructures.

item.mechanism: Severe initial deformation from establishing a constant stress state increases barriers for dynamic recovery and recrystallization.
item.supporting_observation: Samples experience drastic plastic deformation in a short time, leading to severely elongated grains.
item.scope_limits: This is a contributing factor to the increased activation energy, not the primary mechanism for the stress exponent.
quotes: In addition, the samples experience drastic plastic deformation in a short time to establish a constant stress state for subsequent creep deformation.
As a result, some grains are severely elongated, which, in turn, exerts an extra influence on increasing the barriers for dynamic recovery and recrystallization.

item.mechanism: Precipitation hardening contributes to high stress exponents by reducing the effective stress controlling dislocation velocity.
item.supporting_observation: Presence of M23C6 carbides and Cr-rich σ phase precipitates along grain boundaries.
item.scope_limits: Difficult to precisely estimate the boundary obstacle stress due to the complex interaction with recrystallization.
quotes: TEM observations provide clear evidence of dynamic precipitation in HSR. As a result, precipitation hardening may have contributed to the high stress exponents.
The stress controlling the dislocation velocity is reduced to an effective value obtained by subtracting the stress necessary for overcoming precipitates from the applied stress.

By re-plotting the double-logarithm relationship between ε ˙ / exp ( − Q / R T ) and ( σ − σ b o ) / G in HSR, the stress exponents can then be decreased by subtracting the precipitation-hardening portion.

item.mechanism: Creep failure occurs via ductile transgranular rupture despite the presence of brittle precipitates.
item.supporting_observation: Fractographs showing typical ductile rupture with dimples and slip striations, contrary to the expectation of brittle failure.
item.scope_limits: Observed specifically in HSR; the text notes this is contrary to common knowledge regarding brittle precipitates.
item.alternatives_considered: Brittle failure along grain boundaries, which the authors note is generally considered destructive but not observed here.
quotes: It is worth noting that the crept samples fracture in a ductile transgranular manner at high stress, which is contrary to common knowledge, as large amounts of brittle are generally considered to be destructive to the stability of grain boundaries during the tertiary creep stage.
All the fractographs in Figure 10 for HSR from 500 °C to 600 °C exhibit typical ductile rupture, where both the width and depth of dimples increase with temperature.
The ductile creep failure may be associated with the dislocation interactions during high-temperature deformation, which contribute to the progressive generation of vacancies and nucleation of voids.
